book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute

chapters.file: ch07 - A Note on Sources and List of Abbreviations.md

chapters.relation: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

chapters.file: ch13 - 1. How to De-Nazify Nietzsche’s Philosophical Anthropology.md
chapters.relation: Golomb argues the Nazi reading of the will to power as military conquest confuses Nietzsche's Macht (sublimated spiritual power) with Kraft (brute force) and Gewalt (violence), showing through Human, All Too Human and Daybreak that self-overcoming and creative sublimation, not domination, define the Übermensch. He builds a typology of 'positive' versus 'negative' power in which the anti-Semite figures as the vengeful, ressentiment-driven 'slave,' and insists Nietzsche's morality is not naturalistic—power must be transfigured by self-education—so his anthropology stands beyond the eugenic and racial distinctions central to Nazi ideology, even in the misused 'blond beast' passage.

chapters.file: ch14 - 2. Misinterpretation as the Author’s Responsibility (Nietzsche’s fascism, for instance).md
chapters.relation: Berel Lang asks whether an author is responsible for being misinterpreted, defining a 'Fascist Minimum' (priority of the state over the individual, plus natural inequality asserted through war) and testing Nietzsche against it. He finds Nietzsche flatly rejects the first condition—his 'coldest of all cold monsters' attacks on the state and nationalism—and accepts the second only with heavy qualification. Lang locates Nietzsche's partial culpability in a 'Fallacy of Composition' by which readers like Bäumler transposed individual will to power onto the collective state, arguing that Nietzsche, foreseeing this abuse, chose not to 'build a fence' around his meaning and so bears responsibility 'up to a point.'

Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.

Nehamas puts 'Hitler' in scare-quotes to pose an abstract problem—does Nietzsche's ideal of nobility permit the evil hero?—rooting it in the Greek notion of aretê and Plato's Republic. He argues Nietzsche's own doctrine that 'there is no doer behind the deed' (Genealogy I:13) collapses the split between noble soul and noble action, so that deeds confer status; using the case of the police torturing a random woman and the fortuitousness of the Jews' extermination, he contends that when what separates us from victims is mere accident we are their peers, and Nietzsche needs the very doer/deed distinction he attacks in order to reject morality absolutely, so his refusal to condemn the evil hero can be refuted on Nietzschean grounds.

Brinker surveys Duffy-Mittelman, Santaniello, and Yovel to argue that reading Nietzsche as simply pro-Jewish oversimplifies a genuine ambivalence toward the 'Jewish race' running through all periods of Jewish history. He shows that in The Antichrist Nietzsche separates ressentiment from decadence: Jesus is the 'most perfect decadent' incapable of hatred, while Paul and the priests embody ressentiment, and the Jews, being too strong to be decadent, cunningly poison their conquerors with a faith they do not share—an old anti-Semitic stereotype transplanted into new soil. Brinker concludes this ambivalence, plus Nietzsche's post-Zarathustra equation of equality, democracy, and socialism with slave-morality decadence, is exactly what let the Nazis manipulate him.

chapters.file: ch18 - 6. Nietzsche contra Wagner on the Jews.md
chapters.relation: Yovel reads Nietzsche's break with Wagner as a self-overcoming that freed him to hand Wagner's redemptive role—catalyst of a new Dionysian Europe—to the modern secular Jews Wagner despised. He maps a structured ambivalence: fierce anti-anti-Semitism (grounded philosophically in Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism, racism, the state-cult, and ressentiment) coexisting with a fierce critique of ancient 'priestly' Judaism as the genealogical root of Christian slave morality. Contrasting Nietzsche with Wagner's Judaism in Music, he shows Wagner legitimized public hate-speech (dramatized in Siegfried's gratuitous loathing of Mime) while Nietzsche prized self-mastery, so the two men's later Nazi abuse—by Elisabeth and Winifred, the two 'women-priests'—rests on opposite relations to what each actually held.

chapters.file: ch19 - 7. Between the Cross and the Swastika A Nietzschean Perspective.md
chapters.relation: Wistrich answers the charge that Nietzsche was a philosophical godfather of fascism by marshalling his biography and letters—the 'shoot all anti-Semites' twilight notes, the rupture with the anti-Semite Förster and with Wagner, the praise of Heine, Offenbach, and Spinoza. He distinguishes Nietzsche's demonization of Christianity and priestly Judaism as the 'slave revolt in morals' from his admiration for biblical and Diaspora Jews as Europe's toughest race and a possible catalyst of the Übermensch, arguing that the Nazi and Hitlerian echoes (via Table Talk and Rosenberg's forgeries) grossly distort a 'good European' who denounced nationalism, racism, and the state-cult, and would have been repelled by the swastika.

holes.name: Fascism
holes.what: The interwar ultranationalist, anti-liberal, leader-and-state-worshipping political ideology of Mussolini and Hitler.
holes.why: The entire volume, and chapter 10's guiding question, is whether Nietzsche is the 'godfather of fascism'; the taxonomy has no fascism concept, only arendt-totalitarianism, which does not capture fascism specifically.

holes.name: Richard Wagner
holes.what: Composer and cultural ideologue (1813–1883) whose Das Judentum in der Musik and Bayreuth cult fused German nationalism, anti-Semitism, and aesthetics.
holes.why: Chapters 18 and 19 argue centrally that Wagner (not Nietzsche) was the real proto-fascist through whom Nietzsche's own positions are contrasted; the taxonomy has no slug for Wagner as a thinker/figure.
